titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§186–188: The Kereid Divided, Wang Qan's End and Kököchü
part: §§186–188 — The Kereid Divided, Wang Qan's End and Kököchü
about: Three sections that close the war with the Kereid. In §186 Chinggis shares out the conquered Kereid, rewards Taqai-Ba'atur with a hundred Jirgin, and spares Jaqa Gambu, Wang Qan's younger brother, whose two daughters he and his son Tolui have married. In §187 two decrees reward Badai and Kishiliq for their service: they receive Wang Qan's golden tent and the Ongjid Kereid as a guard, and the right to keep their booty and their kill; the Kereid people are shared out until none lacks, and Chinggis winters in the Abji'a-Ködegeri. §188 follows the two fugitives. Wang Qan is killed by a Naiman scout who does not believe who he is; Senggum, abandoned at the Chul by his groom Kököchü, is the subject of the long scene in which Kököchü's wife will not leave him, and Chinggis, hearing the story, favours the wife and has Kököchü cut down for deserting his lord. The grammar to watch is the decree: the formula žarliγ bolurun, the optative -tuγai, the imperative in -dqun, and the conditionals in -γ̇asu; and then a quarrel in nested quotation, where the wife's and husband's lines are not always easy to assign. Several of those lines are hard, and the notes say where. The Mongol readings follow Shiratori; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.t: Tedüi Kereid irge doraitaγ̇ulžu žüg žüg qubijažu talaγ̇ulba.
sentences.l: Those Kereid people, subduing, direction direction dividing, took captive.
sentences.i: He brought the Kereid people to heel, shared them out in every direction, and took them captive.
sentences.n: A converb chain: doraitaγ̇ulžu ‘subduing’ and qubijažu ‘dividing’ (both -žu, ‘-ing’) lead to the one finite verb talaγ̇ulba. The Ming glosses give the sense: doraita- 屈下 ‘bring under’, qubija- 分 ‘divide’, talaγ̇ul- 虜 ‘take captive’; all three stems are inferred, and the -γ̇ul- of the first and last is causative, though talaγ̇ulba simply means ‘took captive’. žüg žüg is ‘side side’, i.e. every way. The subject is not stated; it is Chinggis, carried on from §185. Tedüi (Ming 那些) is the pronoun ‘those’ here.

sentences.t: Suldudai Taγai-Baγ̇atur-un tusa-jin in-ü tula nigen žaγ̇un Žirgin-i ögbe.
sentences.l: Suldudai Taγai-Baγ̇atur's favour, his, because of, one hundred Žirgin(acc) he gave.
sentences.i: In return for the service of Suldudai Taqai-Ba'atur, he gave a hundred Jirgin.
sentences.n: The pattern to learn: [X-genitive] tusa-jin in-ü tula, literally ‘of X, the favour of him, because’, is how this chronicle says ‘for X's service’; it returns in §187 as qojar-un tusa-jin an-u tula. The sentence does not say who received the hundred Jirgin (no dative, and the Ming adds none); Taqai-Ba'atur himself is the natural reading, but that is an inference. Suldudai (Ming 姓(名)) is a clan name. Žirgin-i has the accusative -i (Ming 行).

morph.gloss: Suldudai, of the Suldus, a clan name [姓(名)]
Taqai-Ba'atur, a man's name (baγ̇atur 'hero') [人名 勇士 的]

sentences.t: Basa Čiṅgis Qaγan žarliγ bolurun:
sentences.l: Again Čiṅgis Qaγan, decree becoming:
sentences.i: Again Chinggis Qahan issued a decree:
sentences.n: žarliγ bolurun is a fixed formula: bol- ‘become’ + -urun, ‘when a decree comes to be’, i.e. ‘when he decreed’. The colon opens the speech. The print puts an opening quotation mark before Waṅ-Qān-(n)u in the next unit and never closes it; I close it in the English at the end of the section, and I take the whole of the rest of §186 as the decree.

morph.gloss: Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]

sentences.t: "Waṅ-Qān-(n)u deġü Žaqaγambu žirin ökid ažuγ̇ui.
sentences.l: Waṅ-Qān's younger brother Žaqaγambu, two daughters there were.
sentences.i: “Wang Qan's younger brother Jaqa Gambu had two daughters.
sentences.n: Possession without a verb ‘have’: the possessor stands first in the genitive (Waṅ-Qān-(n)u deġü, ‘Wang Qan's younger brother’) and the verb is a- ‘be’ in the past, ažuγ̇ui, ‘there were’. The (n) of -(n)u is Shiratori's print of the genitive after a stem that already ends in n. ökid is ökin ‘girl’ + plural -d.

morph.gloss: Wang Qan, ruler of the Kereid (Chinese wang 'prince' + qan) [人名的]
Jaqa Gambu, a man's name [人名]

sentences.t: Egečimed in-ü Ibaqa-Beki-ji Čiṅgis Qaγan öġesün aburun
sentences.l: Elder daughter, his, Ibaqa-Beki(acc), Čiṅgis Qaγan himself taking,
sentences.i: His elder daughter Ibaqa-Beki, Chinggis Qahan took for himself,
sentences.n: aburun is ab- ‘take’ + -urun, which meant ‘when …’ in the formula above but here is simply ‘taking’ and leads into the next clause (Ming 要了). öġesün ‘himself’ (Ming 自己) makes the point that he took her for himself. egečimed (Ming 大女) and dölmed (next unit, Ming 次女) are ‘the elder daughter’ and ‘the second daughter’; the forms are obscure (egeči is ‘elder sister’ and -d is usually plural), so each is glossed whole. in-ü is ‘his’, Jaqa Gambu's, set after the noun. Beki is a title, ‘lady’ (cf. Cha'ur-Beki).

sentences.t: dölmed Sorqaγtani-Beki-ji Tolui-(j)a ögbe.
sentences.l: Second daughter, Sorqaγtani-Beki(acc), Tolui-to he gave.
sentences.i: and the second, Sorqaqtani-Beki, he gave to Tolui.
sentences.n: Tolui-(j)a has the dative-locative -(j)a, ‘to’ (Ming 行), the (j) bracketed in the print; Sorqaγtani-Beki-ji has the accusative -ji after a vowel. The two clauses are a contrast, took / gave, with no conjunction.

sentences.t: Tere šiltaγ̇an(i)-jar Žaqaγambu-ji ima-da qarijatan emčü irge ber tumdaγ̇a nögöġe kilgün bol keġežü sojurγažu ese talaγ̇ulba.
sentences.l: That reason-by, Žaqaγambu(acc) to-him, his dependents (and) own people also, whole — ‘second shaft be’ saying, favouring, not took captive.
sentences.i: For that reason, saying ‘Be a second shaft!’, he showed Jaqa Gambu favour, and did not take captive him, his dependents or his own people, one and all.”
sentences.n: A hard sentence; my reading is a first one. The object is Žaqaγambu-ji, then ima-da ‘to him’ (Ming 他行) with his qarijatan (Ming 屬的每, ‘those attached to him’, ‘dependents’) and emčü irge (Ming 梯已 ‘private’, ‘his own people’), ber ‘also’, tumdaγ̇a (Ming 圓全 行, ‘whole’, ‘in full’). Then nögöġe kilgün bol, ‘be a second shaft’ (kilgün Ming 轅條, the shaft of a cart, so a support; bol is the bare-stem imperative), keġežü ‘saying’, sojurγažu ‘showing favour’ and ese talaγ̇ulba, ‘did not take captive’ (ese negates a past act). The forms of qarijatan, tumdaγ̇a and kilgün are uncertain. šiltaγ̇an(i)-jar is ‘cause’ + the instrumental, ‘for that reason’; I take it to point back to the two daughters married into Chinggis's house, but that is my inference. The Ming gives 第二 ‘second’ for nögöġe, so ‘a second’ rather than ‘the other’.

to become, to be (the bare stem is a command, 'be!') [做]

sentences.l: Again Čiṅgis Qaγan, decree becoming:

sentences.n: The same formula as before (žarliγ bolurun). The decree that follows is in direct speech; the print opens a quotation before Badai, and the English follows it.

sentences.t: "Badai, Kišiliγ qojar-un tusa-jin an-u tula Waṅ-Qān-(n)u altan terme saγ̇uγsaγ̇ar altan kürüġe ajaγa saba asaraγsad haran selte Oṅγ̇ožid Kereid-i kešigten an-u boltuγai;
sentences.l: Badai, Kišiliγ, of the two favour their because of, Waṅ-Qān's gold tent standing-as, gold wine-set cup vessel tending people with, Oṅγ̇ožid Kereid(acc), guard their let be;
sentences.i: “Badai, Kishiliq! In return for the service of you two, Wang Qan's golden tent just as it stands, with the people who tended the golden wine-vessels, cups and bowls, and the Ongjid Kereid as your guard: let it be so;
sentences.n: Opens with the pattern from §186 (qojar-un tusa-jin an-u tula, ‘because of the favour of the two’). The speech names Badai and Kishiliq, then speaks of them in the third person (an-u, ‘their’), and later turns to them with a plural imperative (-dqun); I put ‘you’ in the English. saγ̇uγsaγ̇ar is saγ̇u- ‘sit’ (of a tent, ‘stand pitched’) + past participle -γsan + the instrumental -γ̇ar: ‘as it stands’ (Ming 全具 ‘complete with fittings’); the same ending appears below in oluγsaγ̇ar. The four vessel words (altan kürüġe ajaγa saba) are Ming 金 酒局 器 皿, ‘gold wine-set, cup, dish’; kürüġe is uncertain. asaraγsad haran selte is ‘with the people who tended (them)’. How the unmarked tent and its household relate to the Ongjid Kereid (accusative) and to the optative boltuγai ‘let it be’ is my reading: both are things given to the two. kešigten (Ming 宿衞的每) is the guard of the household.

past participle plural (-γsan + -d): those who have -ed

sentences.t: qorčilaγ̇ulžu ötögleġülžü uruγ-un uruγ-a kürtele darqalan žirγadqun;
sentences.l: Quiver-bearing-causing, cup-offering-causing, offspring's to offspring until, free, rejoice!
sentences.i: Have them bear the bow and offer the cup for you, and be free and glad, down to your children's children.
sentences.n: qorčilaγ̇ulžu and ötögleġülžü are causative converbs (-γ̇ul-, -ġül-, ‘having (them) do’), glossed by the Ming 敎帶弓箭着 ‘have them wear the bow and arrows’ and 喝盞着 ‘have them call the cup’; the stems qorčila- and ötögle- are inferred from those glosses and point to the quiver-bearer's and cup-bearer's offices of a household guard. The ones made to serve are the Ongjid Kereid of the last unit. uruγ-un uruγ-a kürtele, ‘down to the offspring of the offspring’, is the formula for a grant that descends. darqalan: darqan is a free man exempt from dues, but the Ming 自在 says only ‘free’, so the analysis is uncertain. žirγadqun is žirγa- ‘be glad’ + -dqun, the polite plural imperative (Ming 您).

morph.gloss: to bear the bow and quiver (qorči 'quiver-bearer'; stem inferred from the Ming) [敎帶弓箭着]
to offer the cup, call the toast (stem inferred from the Ming) [喝︀盞着]
to be glad, to rejoice [快樂您]
imperative, polite plural: please, do (Ming 您)

sentences.t: olon dain-dur qaγ̇uluγ̇asu olža oluγ̇asu oluγsaγ̇ar abudqun.
sentences.l: Many enemy-against, if rushing, booty if getting, got-as, take!
sentences.i: If, rushing against the many enemies, you win booty, take it as you win it.
sentences.n: Two conditionals (-γ̇asu, ‘if’), qaγ̇uluγ̇asu (Ming 奔呵, ‘if (you) rush’; the stem is guessed from the gloss) and oluγ̇asu ‘if (you) get’, then the main verb abudqun. oluγsaγ̇ar is ol- + -γsan + -γ̇ar, ‘according to what is got’ (Ming 得了的依着), the same ending as saγ̇uγsaγ̇ar above: ‘take it as you get it’, i.e. keep what you win. dain-dur is ‘against the enemy’ (dative-locative).

morph.gloss: to rush forth, dash (stem inferred from the Ming 奔; uncertain) [奔呵]
to find, get [得了的 依着]
imperative, polite plural: please, do (Ming 您)

sentences.t: Uraγ̇a göreġesün alaγ̇asu alaγsaγ̇ar abudqun" keġen žarliγ bolba.
sentences.l: Wild game, if killing, killed-as take!” saying, a decree became.
sentences.i: If you kill game, take it as you kill it.” So he decreed.
sentences.n: Parallel to the last unit. Uraγ̇a is printed with a capital as the start of a sentence inside the quotation; the Ming 野 ‘wild’ is the only evidence for it, so ‘wild beasts’ with göreġesün 獸 is my reading. The privilege is to keep one's kill as one's own, as with booty. keġen žarliγ bolba, ‘saying, a decree was made’, closes the quotation: keġen is keġe- ‘say’ + -n.

morph.gloss: imperative, polite plural: please, do (Ming 您)

sentences.t: Basa Čiṅgis Qaγan žarliγ bolurun:
sentences.l: Again Čiṅgis Qaγan, decree becoming:
sentences.i: Again Chinggis Qahan issued a decree:
sentences.n: The same opening formula for a second decree to the same men.

morph.gloss: Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]

sentences.t: "Badai, Kišiliγ qojar-un amin žaγ̇ura tusa kürgegsen-ü tula müṅke teṅgeri-de igeġegdežü Kereid irge doroidaγ̇ulžu ündür-ün oron-dur kürbe-že.
sentences.l: Badai, Kišiliγ, of the two in the midst of life favour having brought because of, eternal Heaven-by being helped, Kereid people subduing, of the high to the seat reached indeed.
sentences.i: “Badai, Kishiliq! Because you two did me service at risk of your lives, I, helped by Eternal Heaven, have subdued the Kereid people and come to the high seat.
sentences.n: amin žaγ̇ura (Ming 性命 其間) is literally ‘in the midst of life’; ‘at risk of your lives’ is my reading of it. kürgegsen-ü tula puts the past participle in the genitive before tula, ‘because of having rendered (service)’; that ‘because’ governs only the service, and the Heaven clause is a separate statement. Teṅgeri-de: the dative-locative on ‘Heaven’ marks the doer of a passive, igeġegdežü ‘being helped’ (igeġe-, stem inferred from the Ming 護助, + passive -gde- + -žü). doroidaγ̇ulžu is the causative of ‘submit’, as doraitaγ̇ulžu in §186, in another spelling. ündür-ün oron-dur (Ming 名的 位裏) I take as ‘to the high seat’ (ündür ‘high’), the throne or rank; the Ming reads ündür as 名 ‘name’, so ‘the seat of renown’ is possible; the speaker is Chinggis, as the min-u ‘my’ of the next unit shows, so ‘I’. The ending -že on kürbe is the particle ‘indeed’ (Ming 也者).

morph.gloss: to bring to, render (kür- 'reach' made causative; uncertain) [到了的]
because of, on account of (postposition) [上頭]
Heaven, the sky as a power [天 行]
to protect, help (stem inferred from the Ming) [被護助着]
the Kereid, a people (the -d is probably plural) [種(名)]
people, subjects (a form of irgen) [百姓]
to submit, be subdued (stem uncertain) [屈下了着]
high, tall (Ming 名的 'of the name') [名的]

sentences.t: Mönö qoina uruγ-un uruγ-a min-u oron-dur saγ̇užu ene metü tusa kürgegsed-i ulam ulam uqatuγai" keġen žarliγ bolba.
sentences.l: Long after, offspring's to offspring, my seat-in sitting, this like favour those who have brought(acc), more more let know!” saying, a decree became.
sentences.i: In all the time to come, let the children of my children, sitting in my seat, take ever greater account of those who have done such service!” So he decreed.
sentences.n: mönö qoina (Ming 久 後) is ‘long afterwards’; mönö elsewhere is ‘tomorrow’, so the Ming is the guide. kürgegsed-i is the past participle in the plural with the accusative, ‘those who have rendered’, and tusa … kürge- is ‘to render service’ (as in the last unit). uqa- is ‘know, understand’ and uqatuγai the optative; with ulam ulam (Ming 轉轉, ‘more and more’) the sense is ‘take note of, remember’, which I have rendered ‘take account of’. The decree provides that the favour done will be recognised by every later ruler.

to bring to, render (kür- 'reach' made causative; uncertain) [到了的(每)行]

sentences.t: Kereid irge daγ̇uližu ken-e ber ese dutatala tügeġeldübe.
sentences.l: Kereid people plundering, whom-to even not lacking, shared out.
sentences.i: Having carried off the Kereid people, he shared them out so that no one went short.
sentences.n: daγ̇uližu (Ming 擄着) ‘plundering’, then ken-e ber ese dutatala, ‘to anyone also, not lacking’: ese with the converb in -tala, ‘without anyone lacking’. tügeġeldübe (Ming 共散與了) has the reciprocal -ldü-, ‘to all in common’; its stem tügeġe- is inferred from the Ming. The subject, Chinggis, is not stated.

sentences.t: Tümen-Tübeġen-i tügeġeldüžü tügelete abulčaba.
sentences.l: Tümen-Tübeġen(acc) sharing out, until enough, took jointly.
sentences.i: The Tümen-Tübegen they shared out among them until there was enough, and took them jointly.
sentences.n: tügelete (Ming 勾了, ‘enough’) is probably tügele- ‘be sufficient’ + -te for -tele, ‘until it was enough’; uncertain. abulčaba is ab- ‘take’ + -ulča- ‘jointly’ + -ba (Ming 共要了). Tümen-Tübeġen (Ming 萬 姓(名), tümen is ‘ten thousand’) is a people name. The subject is again not stated.

to be enough, be complete (stem inferred from the Ming 勾) [勾了]

sentences.t: Olon-Doṅγaid uquγa üdür-e ülü kürgen talaγ̇ulba-že.
sentences.l: Olon-Doṅγaid whole day-in not reaching, had taken captive indeed.
sentences.i: They kept taking the Olon-Dongqaid captive all day and still did not come to the end of them.
sentences.n: Uncertain. ülü kürgen … talaγ̇ulba-že, Ming 不到敎虜了也者: ‘not reaching, they had (them) taken captive’. I read kürgen (kürge- ‘bring to’) as ‘reaching an end’, which would fit the previous sentences' point (so many captives that the sharing could not be finished); it may rather be ‘not delivering (them all)’. uquγa üdür-e (Ming 整日行) is ‘all day’, with the dative-locative -e. že is the particle ‘indeed’.

morph.gloss: Olon-Dongqaid, a clan name (olon 'many') [多 姓(名)]
to bring to, deliver (kür- 'reach' made causative; uncertain) [到]
to plunder, take captive (stem inferred from the Ming) [敎虜︀了 也者︀]

sentences.t: Čisutu tonoγ abuγči Žirgin baγ̇atud-i žisüžü qubijažu kürgeldün jadaba.
sentences.l: Blood-having, plunder taking, Žirgin heroes(acc), cutting open, dividing, delivering to one another, were unable.
sentences.i: Those bloody takers of plunder, the Jirgin warriors, were cut open and divided into shares, but they could not be handed round to one another.
sentences.n: Hard; a first reading. Čisutu tonoγ abuγči (Ming 血有的 剝脫 好要的) reads as an epithet of the Jirgin: čisu ‘blood’ + -tu ‘having’ (the possessive pattern), tonoγ ‘stripping’ (Ming 剝脫), abuγči ‘taker’ (ab- + -γči). žisüžü (Ming 𠠍開着 ‘cutting open’) is a guessed stem. kürgeldün is kürge- ‘bring to’ + -ldü- (one another) + -n, and jadaba ‘were unable’. The sentence says the Jirgin could not all be shared out; who does the cutting is not stated, and whether the object (baγ̇atud-i, accusative) is the Jirgin or their share is open.

morph.gloss: stripping, plunder (Ming 剝脫 'strip off') [剝脫]
to cut open, slit (stem inferred from the Ming 𠠍開) [𠠍開着]
to divide, share out (stem inferred from the Ming) [分着]
to bring to, deliver (kür- 'reach' made causative; uncertain) [共到的]

sentences.t: Kereid irge tedüi qoruγ̇ažu tere übül Abžiγ̇a-Ködegeri übülžebe.
sentences.l: Kereid people those ending, that winter Abžiγ̇a-Ködegeri wintered.
sentences.i: Having made an end of the Kereid people, he wintered that winter at Abji'a-Ködegeri.
sentences.n: qoruγ̇ažu (Ming 廢了着, ‘abolished’) is a guessed stem; ‘having made an end of’. übülžebe is übül ‘winter’ + the verbal -že- + past -be, ‘wintered’ (Ming 住冬了). Abžiγ̇a-Ködegeri is, by the Ming, a mountain name (山名); the place takes no case ending. tere übül, ‘that winter’, is the time. Tedüi is again the pronoun ‘those’.

morph.gloss: the Kereid, a people (the -d is probably plural) [種名]
people, subjects (a form of irgen) [百姓]
to put an end to, abolish (stem inferred from the Ming 廢) [廢了着]
Abji'a-Ködegeri, a mountain name (Ming 山名) [山名]

sentences.t: Waṅ-Qān Seṅgüm qojar bejes(i)-jen daižižu γarču oduγ̇ad
sentences.l: Waṅ-Qān, Seṅgüm, the two, own persons, turning hostile, going out, having gone,
sentences.i: Wang Qan and Senggum, the two of them, in revolt and bare of all but their own persons, went out and away,
sentences.n: A flight narrative opens; the long converb chain is broken here into two units. daižižu ‘turning hostile’ (daiži-, from dain ‘enemy’; Ming 反), γarču ‘going out’, oduγ̇ad ‘having gone’. bejes(i)-jen is beje ‘body’ + plural + reflexive -(i)jen, ‘their own persons’ (Ming 罄身 ‘bare body’), i.e. with nothing else; the bracketed (i) is Shiratori's linking vowel. Seṅgüm is Wang Qan's son (as in the earlier parts).

sentences.i: As Wang Qan, thirsty, was about to enter the water Negün-Usun in Didig-Saqal, he fell in with Qori-Sübechi, a scout of the Naiman.
sentences.n: oroqu bolun is the participle -qu + bolun, ‘when about to enter’ (Ming 入 做), the same pattern as neġükü bolun elsewhere. qaṅγažu ‘being thirsty’ (Ming 渴着). orožuγ̇u is oro- ‘enter’ + -žuγ̇u, Ming 入了來 ‘came in’, here ‘came into the hands of’. Negün-Usun-a is, by the Ming (水名 水行), ‘to the water named Negün-Usun’; Didig-Saqal-un (Ming 地名 的) names the place it lies in.

sentences.t: "Bi Waṅ-Qān bijü" kēġesü ülü tanin ese büširežü tende alažuγ̇u.
sentences.l: ‘I Waṅ-Qān am’, if he said, not recognising, not believing, there killed.
sentences.i: “I am Wang Qan,” he said, but Qori-Sübechi did not know him, and, not believing him, killed him there.

sentences.i: Wild asses, bitten by gadflies, were standing about looking for water; Senggum dismounted and crept up on them.

sentences.t: "Altatai-ji emüsküi-dür amtatai-ji ideküi-dür Kököčü min-u keġekü büleġe.
sentences.l: Gold-having(acc) at wearing, flavour-having(acc) at eating, Kököčü ‘mine’ saying-one there was.
sentences.i: “When he put on gold, when he ate savoury food, he used to say, ‘Kököchü is mine.’
sentences.n: Uncertain. Altatai-ji and amtatai-ji are ‘gold-having’ and ‘flavour-having’ (-tai, ‘having’) in the accusative, objects of emüsküi ‘wearing’ and ideküi ‘eating’ (participle -küi + -dür, ‘at the time of’): the wife is recalling the good days. I take the one who ‘used to say’ to be Senggum, claiming Kököchü as his own man; the Ming gives no subject, and it may instead be Kököchü who used to say ‘my (lord)’. keġekü büleġe, ‘was one saying’ (Ming 說的有來), is a habitual past. Altatai (Ming 金 有的行) drops the n of altan before -tai.
